nodes.label: The Buyids take Baghdad
nodes.full: Ahmad ibn Buya marches into Baghdad in 945 and takes over as 'commander of commanders', leaving the Abbasid caliph on his throne as a pensioner — the event this folio picks up the morning after.

nodes.label: Genghis Khan unifies the Mongols
nodes.full: Temujin is proclaimed Genghis Khan over a unified Mongol confederation in 1206, building the army and state that will overrun the Khwarazm-Shah's empire within fifteen years and, two generations later, sack Baghdad.

nodes.label: The Mongols shatter the Qipchaq Turks
nodes.full: A separate Mongol campaign into the steppe north of the Black Sea breaks the Qipchaq (Cuman) confederation in 1237-40, throwing tens of thousands of steppe people onto the slave markets that supply Cairo.

nodes.label: Al-Muti', al-Ta'i' and al-Qadir
nodes.full: Under Shia overlords the Sunni caliphs kept the ceremony and lost the substance — pensioned, occasionally blinded and deposed. Al-Qadir (r.991-1031) issued the 'Qadiri Creed' (1018), a public statement of Sunni orthodoxy that was one of the few acts of religious authority still open to him.

nodes.label: Al-Qa'im and the Fatimid year
nodes.full: Al-Qa'im's long reign spanned the fall of the Buyids and the arrival of the Seljuks. In 1058 the pro-Fatimid general al-Basasiri seized Baghdad and had the sermon read for the Cairo caliph for a year — the closest the Abbasid line came to ending before the Mongols. Tughril's Seljuks restored him in 1059.

nodes.label: Al-Muqtadi and al-Mustazhir
nodes.full: These caliphs reigned during the Seljuk apogee under Malik-Shah and, after 1092, its collapse. The First Crusade took Jerusalem in al-Mustazhir's reign; a delegation of Syrian refugees came to Baghdad to appeal for help and got a sympathetic hearing and nothing else.

nodes.label: Al-Mustarshid — the caliph takes the field
nodes.full: With Seljuk power fracturing, al-Mustarshid raised an army and tried to make the caliphate a territorial power in Iraq again. He was defeated and captured by the sultan Mas'ud in 1135 and then murdered by Nizari Assassins; his son al-Rashid was deposed within a year.

nodes.label: Al-Muqtafi and al-Mustanjid
nodes.full: These caliphs finished what al-Mustarshid began: they defended Baghdad against a Seljuk siege (1157), pushed the last sultan's forces out of central Iraq, and ruled the region directly. For the first time in two centuries the caliph was also a functioning prince.

nodes.label: Al-Nasir to al-Musta'sim
nodes.full: Al-Nasir ruled 45 years and rebuilt a real Abbasid state in Iraq, using diplomacy, an army, and a reorganised chivalric order (futuwwa) he headed himself. His successors built the great Mustansiriyya law college (1234) — and in 1258 the indecisive al-Musta'sim faced Hulagu, refused to submit, and lost his city and his life.

nodes.label: Mu'izz al-Dawla and Adud al-Dawla
nodes.full: Mu'izz al-Dawla marched into Baghdad in 945 and took the title 'commander of commanders', keeping the caliph as a pensioner. Under Adud al-Dawla (d.983) the Buyid confederation reached its height — a wealthy, cultivated, Shia court that patronised Ibn Sina's generation and built the great Baghdad hospital.

nodes.label: Buyid decline and the rise of Ghazna
nodes.full: The Buyids fell into family war and lost their grip on Iraq. To the east, Mahmud of Ghazna built a Sunni military empire funded by plundering raids into India, received the title 'sultan' from the caliph, and kept Firdawsi and al-Biruni at his court.

nodes.label: Tughril Beg — the Seljuks take Baghdad
nodes.full: The Seljuk Turks defeated the Ghaznavids at Dandanaqan in 1040, overran Iran, and in 1055 Tughril entered Baghdad, expelled the last Buyid, took the title sultan from the caliph and married into his family.

nodes.label: Alp Arslan, Malik-Shah and Nizam al-Mulk
nodes.full: For thirty years the empire ran from the Aegean to Central Asia, governed by the vizier Nizam al-Mulk, who founded the Nizamiyya madrasas. Alp Arslan captured the Byzantine emperor at Manzikert (1071). Then in 1092 both Malik-Shah and Nizam al-Mulk died within weeks, and the empire came apart.

nodes.label: The succession wars and the atabeg states
nodes.full: Malik-Shah's sons and grandsons fought for decades; the empire split into a Great Seljuk sultanate under Sanjar, a Seljuk sultanate of Iraq, and the Seljuks of Rum. Real power in the provinces passed to the atabegs, who founded dynasties of their own: the Zangids, the Bori, others.

nodes.label: The Khwarazm-Shahs
nodes.full: After Sanjar the eastern Islamic world passed to the Khwarazm-Shahs. Ala al-Din Muhammad II built a huge, brittle empire, quarrelled with the caliph al-Nasir over Baghdad, and in 1218 executed a Mongol trade mission — the act that brought Genghis Khan west.

nodes.label: Hulagu and the Ilkhanate
nodes.full: Genghis Khan's grandson Hulagu was sent to finish the west: he destroyed the Nizari Assassin state (Alamut fell in 1256), then in February 1258 took Baghdad, sacked it, and killed the last caliph. The Ilkhanate he founded ruled Iran and Iraq until the 1330s.

nodes.label: Dandanaqan and the Seljuk takeover of Iran
nodes.full: The Seljuk Turks broke the Ghaznavid army at Dandanaqan in 1040 and within fifteen years held all of Iran and had entered Baghdad — less a single conquest than a migration under arms.

nodes.label: The Basasiri revolt
nodes.full: A Buyid Turkish general, Arslan al-Basasiri, allied with Fatimid Cairo, seized Baghdad, imprisoned the caliph and had the sermon read in the Fatimid name for a year (1058-59). Tughril's Seljuks retook the city and restored al-Qa'im.

nodes.label: Manzikert
nodes.full: Alp Arslan's defeat and capture of the Byzantine emperor Romanos IV was not decisive in itself — but the Byzantine civil war that followed left Anatolia undefended, and Turkish nomads poured in and stayed.

nodes.label: The First Crusade and the fall of Jerusalem
nodes.full: A Latin Christian army exploited the wreck of Seljuk unity to take Antioch (1098) and Jerusalem (1099), massacring much of the population. The Muslim world took nearly fifty years to mount a serious response.

nodes.label: Qatwan — the eastern collapse
nodes.full: The Qara Khitai, a Buddhist dynasty of refugees from north China, routed the Great Seljuk sultan Sanjar in Transoxiana. It ended Seljuk power in the east and put a non-Muslim empire over Central Asian Muslims.

nodes.label: The unification of Syria under Nur al-Din
nodes.full: Zangi's capture of Edessa in 1144 triggered the disastrous Second Crusade. Zangi's son Nur al-Din then took Damascus (1154) and, through Shirkuh and Saladin, Egypt (1169) — assembling in one hand the resources to face the Franks.

nodes.label: Hattin and the Third Crusade
nodes.full: Saladin destroyed the crusader field army at Hattin and retook Jerusalem eighty-eight years after its loss. The Third Crusade under Richard of England recovered the coast but could not retake the city; the war ended in a truce.
nodes.src: Baha al-Din ibn Shaddad; Imad al-Din al-Isfahani

nodes.label: The war of the dagger
nodes.full: With no territory large enough to field an army, the Nizari Ismailis seized mountain fortresses and made assassination a systematic instrument of state — the vizier Nizam al-Mulk in 1092, the caliph al-Mustarshid in 1135, and dozens of emirs and princes.

nodes.label: The destruction of Khwarazm
nodes.full: After the Khwarazm-Shah executed his envoys, Genghis Khan turned the whole Mongol army west. Bukhara and Samarqand fell in 1220; Merv, Nishapur and Herat were sacked and their populations put to the sword.

nodes.label: The sack of Baghdad and the check at Ayn Jalut
nodes.full: Hulagu took Baghdad after a short siege in February 1258, sacked it, and had the caliph killed. Two years later a Mamluk army defeated a Mongol detachment at Ayn Jalut — the first serious check to the Mongol advance.

nodes.label: Al-Mawardi writes the constitution of the caliphate
nodes.full: Al-Mawardi's 'Ordinances of Government' set out the classic Sunni theory of the caliphate — its qualifications, its powers, the delegation of authority — at the very moment the caliph had none of them. Its real achievement was to make room in the law for a sultan who held power the caliph had 'delegated'.

nodes.label: The sultanate and Nizam al-Mulk's manual of rule
nodes.full: Under the Seljuks the division became formal: the caliph is the imam of the faith, the sultan holds the sword and the state. Nizam al-Mulk's 'Book of Government' codified how that state should work.

nodes.label: The madrasa as an instrument of state
nodes.full: Nizam al-Mulk founded a network of endowed law colleges — the Nizamiyya madrasas — to train Sunni scholars, staff the courts, and counter Shia and Ismaili teaching. The ulama were increasingly on the state's payroll.

nodes.label: The iqta becomes the military-fiscal system
nodes.full: Under the Buyids and Seljuks the assignment of a district's tax revenue to a soldier in place of pay became the normal way to maintain an army — tying the military to the land and weakening the central treasury.

nodes.label: The waqf — the endowment that built the Islamic city
nodes.full: The pious endowment — property whose income is permanently dedicated to a mosque, madrasa, hospital or fountain — was the legal engine of urban Islamic life. In this period it became ubiquitous, funding almost every public building.

nodes.label: Al-Nasir's futuwwa order
nodes.full: The caliph al-Nasir took over the urban young-men's fraternities (futuwwa), had himself initiated as their head, and issued membership to rulers from Anatolia to Egypt — chivalry as foreign policy.

nodes.label: The Sunni revival
nodes.full: After a century in which Shia dynasties ruled most of the Islamic world, the Seljuks backed a deliberate reassertion of Sunnism: the madrasa network, an alliance of Ash'ari theology with Shafi'i and Hanafi law, and pressure on Mu'tazilism and Shiism alike.

nodes.label: Al-Ghazali — law, theology and Sufism reconciled
nodes.full: The most celebrated jurist of his day, al-Ghazali left his Baghdad chair in a crisis of doubt and wrote the 'Revival of the Religious Sciences' — a synthesis that gave Sufi practice a secure place inside Sunni orthodoxy. His 'Incoherence of the Philosophers' checked falsafa's prestige for centuries.

nodes.label: The Sufi orders become institutions
nodes.full: Sufism moved from a personal path to organised brotherhoods (tariqas) with a founding master, a chain of authority and a lodge. Abd al-Qadir al-Jilani's Qadiriyya and Ahmad al-Rifa'i's Rifa'iyya, both centred in Iraq, were among the first and largest.

nodes.label: Ibn Arabi and the unity of being
nodes.full: An Andalusi who settled in the Near East, Ibn Arabi produced the most ambitious speculative mysticism in Islam — the doctrine, later called wahdat al-wujud, that all existence is a single reality manifesting the divine names.

nodes.label: The Shia academy moves to Najaf
nodes.full: Under Buyid protection the Twelver scholars of Baghdad built a rational Shia theology and completed the four canonical Shia hadith books. After the Seljuks came and Sunni mobs burned al-Tusi's library, he moved the school to Najaf.

nodes.label: The Nizari 'Resurrection' at Alamut
nodes.full: In 1164 the Nizari imam at Alamut proclaimed the qiyama — the Resurrection — declaring that the age of the sacred law was over and that his community now lived in the spiritual reality the law had only symbolised.

nodes.label: Ibn al-Jawzi and the Hanbali preachers of Baghdad
nodes.full: The Hanbali school, strongest in Baghdad, produced in Ibn al-Jawzi a phenomenally productive scholar and popular preacher who attacked Sufi and philosophical error and defended a scripture-first, reason-wary piety.

nodes.label: The Church of the East reaches the Mongols
nodes.full: While the Church of the East contracted in Iraq, it expanded east: whole Turkic peoples of the steppe were Christian, and Mongol royal women of that faith sat at the centre of the empire that destroyed Baghdad.

nodes.label: The four-iwan plan and the Seljuk dome
nodes.full: Seljuk builders fixed the plan that Iranian mosques and madrasas kept for a thousand years — a courtyard with a great vaulted hall on each of its four sides — and raised over the Isfahan mihrab a brick double-shell dome, a landmark of structural design.
nodes.src: the Masjid-i Jami of Isfahan; Hillenbrand (1994)

nodes.label: The tomb tower and the muqarnas vault
nodes.full: The soaring brick tomb tower of Gunbad-i Qabus (1006) opens a great age of Iranian funerary architecture. In the same period the muqarnas — the honeycomb of niches bridging a square room to a round dome — was invented and spread across the Islamic world.

nodes.label: The Baghdad school of painting
nodes.full: The first great Arab painting appears in illustrated books of the early 13th century — al-Hariri's 'Assemblies' with crowded, observed scenes of markets and caravans. It flourished for two generations and was cut off by the Mongol sack.

nodes.label: Mosul inlaid brass
nodes.full: Mosul metalworkers brought the inlaying of brass with silver and copper to a peak never matched. The Mongol advance drove the masters to Cairo and Damascus, carrying the 'Mosul style' with them.

nodes.label: The ceramic revolution of Kashan
nodes.full: The potters of Kashan perfected a hard white 'stonepaste' body covered with overglaze enamel painting (mina'i) and metallic lustre, producing figural bowls, star tiles and mosque mihrabs of extraordinary refinement.

nodes.label: The Persian renaissance and the Arabic silver age
nodes.full: Firdawsi completed the 'Shahnama', 50,000 verses of Persian national epic, around 1010. In Arabic, al-Mutanabbi at the Hamdanid court of Aleppo was hailed as the greatest of all poets, and the blind al-Ma'arri wrote verse of unflinching doubt.

nodes.label: Ibn Sina — the summit of falsafa
nodes.full: Physician, philosopher and vizier, Ibn Sina wrote the 'Canon of Medicine' — a standard textbook into the 17th century — and the 'Book of Healing', whose account of the soul shaped both later Islamic thought and Latin scholasticism.

nodes.label: Al-Biruni — the measure of the world
nodes.full: Carried to Ghazna as a captive scholar, al-Biruni learned Sanskrit and wrote 'India', the first attempt by anyone to describe another civilisation's science and religion on their own terms. He also measured the Earth's radius from a single mountain.

nodes.label: Al-Ghazali against the philosophers
nodes.full: Al-Ghazali's 'Incoherence of the Philosophers' argued that on twenty points the Aristotelians of Islam contradicted reason and revelation. The Andalusi Ibn Rushd's reply was read more in Latin Europe than in the Muslim east.

nodes.label: Omar Khayyam — cubic equations and a calendar
nodes.full: Khayyam gave the first systematic treatment of cubic equations, solving them geometrically, and headed the commission that produced the Jalali calendar of 1079 — more accurate than the Gregorian calendar adopted five centuries later.

nodes.label: Al-Jazari's Book of Ingenious Mechanical Devices
nodes.full: Al-Jazari's treatise describes fifty machines with the drawings and tolerances to build them: water-raising pumps with a true crankshaft, the elephant clock, and musical robots that could be reprogrammed.

nodes.label: Ibn al-Athir and the historians of the catastrophe
nodes.full: Ibn al-Athir's 'Complete History' is the great narrative synthesis of the medieval Islamic world, and its account of the Mongol conquest — 'a calamity such as had not been seen before' — is a civilisation watching itself attacked.

nodes.label: The Fihrist — a catalogue of everything written
nodes.full: Ibn al-Nadim, a Baghdad bookseller, compiled the 'Fihrist' — an annotated index of every book he knew to exist in Arabic, a snapshot of the entire intellectual production of the Islamic world at its peak.

nodes.label: The economic centre leaves Iraq
nodes.full: As Baghdad declined, the weight of the Islamic economy moved to Fatimid then Ayyubid Cairo and to the Seljuk capital of Isfahan. Iraq went from the richest province of the caliphate to a contested march.

nodes.label: The end of the Sawad
nodes.full: The great Nahrawan canal was breached in a war in 937 and never repaired. Over the next three centuries the irrigation grid of southern Iraq decayed, so that when the Mongols came in 1258 they finished a land that was already half ruined.

nodes.label: The militarised land
nodes.full: With the iqta the dominant form of military pay, land and its revenue passed increasingly into the hands of Turkish soldiers and their households. The free village community weakened and the state's cash income shrank.

nodes.label: The Red Sea route and the Karimi merchants
nodes.full: The long-distance spice trade with India and the Far East shifted from the Gulf, which had run it under the Abbasids, to the Red Sea and Cairo. A wealthy guild-like body of merchants, the Karimis, came to dominate it.

nodes.label: Commerce through the Crusades
nodes.full: For two centuries Italian merchant colonies in the crusader ports and in Alexandria carried European silver and cloth east and Asian spices, sugar and glass west. The Frankish states were as much a commercial interface as a battlefront.

nodes.label: Papermaking crosses to the Mediterranean
nodes.full: The paper industry spread west from Iraq to Syria and Egypt, then across North Africa to Fez, and to Muslim Spain, where the mills of Xativa were exporting to Christian Europe by the 12th century.

nodes.label: The crankshaft and the reciprocating pump
nodes.full: Al-Jazari's water-raising machine used a true crankshaft to convert the rotation of a water-wheel into the back-and-forth of a double-acting suction pump — centuries before the same mechanism's European use.

nodes.label: The Persian windmill
nodes.full: The earliest windmills for which there is clear evidence were vertical-axis machines on the windy plains of eastern Iran, walled to catch the seasonal wind and used to grind grain and pump water.

nodes.label: The counterweight trebuchet and the citadel
nodes.full: The counterweight trebuchet spread through the Islamic world in the century of the Crusades, and rulers answered it by rebuilding their cities' citadels on a massive new scale. Fortification and artillery escalated together.

nodes.label: The Maragha observatory
nodes.full: The year after Baghdad fell, Hulagu founded for Nasir al-Din al-Tusi an observatory with a library and a staff of astronomers from across Asia. It was the first true scientific research institution of its kind.

nodes.label: Distillation, glass and the perfume trade
nodes.full: The alembic still supported industries in rosewater and medicinal spirits, traded across the region and into Europe. Syrian and Iraqi glassmakers developed enamelled and gilded wares.

nodes.label: The Turkish migration into the Middle East
nodes.full: The Seljuk conquest brought not just a ruling house but the Oghuz Turkish tribes behind it. After Manzikert (1071) they poured into Anatolia and stayed; within two centuries the plateau was Turkish and Muslim.

nodes.label: The Crusades as contact
nodes.full: Two centuries of Franks living in Syria and Palestine produced real exchange: crusader castle-building learned from and taught Muslim engineers; sugar-cane cultivation followed the crusaders home.

nodes.label: The sciences pass to Latin Europe
nodes.full: Just as al-Ghazali was checking philosophy's prestige in the east, translators in Toledo and Sicily were turning the Arabic corpus — Ibn Sina's Canon, al-Khwarizmi's algebra, Ibn Rushd's Aristotle — into Latin.

nodes.label: The overland route and the Central Asian cities
nodes.full: Before the Mongols, the great cities of Khurasan and Transoxiana were among the largest and richest in the Islamic world, hubs of trade and centres of learning that produced al-Biruni, al-Bukhari and Ibn Sina.

nodes.label: The scholars flee the Mongols
nodes.full: The Mongol conquest drove a generation of scholars, craftsmen and Sufis west and east — to Mamluk Cairo, which became the new centre of Sunni learning, and to the Delhi Sultanate.

nodes.label: The Mongols and the wider world
nodes.full: As the Mongols advanced, popes and kings sent friars to their court hoping for an ally against Islam. The Ilkhanate would spend decades courting the Latin west against the Mamluks — an alliance that never quite happened.

nodes.label: The Shi'i century
nodes.full: For a hundred years the major powers of the Islamic world were Shia: the Fatimid caliphate in Egypt, the Buyids in Iraq and western Iran, the Hamdanids in Syria, the Qarmatians in eastern Arabia. The Sunni Abbasid caliph was a protected relic in the middle of it.

nodes.label: The Seljuk restoration
nodes.full: Tughril's entry into Baghdad reversed the Shi'i century: a Sunni Turkic power now stood behind the caliph, and the sultanate became the permanent secular counterpart to the caliphal office.

nodes.label: The Crusades
nodes.full: The Latin west's two-century attempt to hold Jerusalem and a strip of the Syrian coast was a chronic frontier war rather than an existential threat — but it forged the careers of Nur al-Din and Saladin and hardened the ideology of jihad.

nodes.label: The Ayyubids and the Mamluk coup
nodes.full: Saladin abolished the Fatimid caliphate in 1171 and built an Ayyubid confederation over Egypt and Syria. In 1250 the Turkish slave-soldiers of the Egyptian army killed the last Ayyubid and took power themselves — the Mamluk Sultanate.

nodes.label: The Mongol cataclysm
nodes.full: In forty years the Mongols destroyed Khwarazm, sacked Baghdad and ended the caliphate, and set up the Ilkhanate over Iran and Iraq. The advance was finally checked by the Mamluks at Ayn Jalut in 1260.

nodes.label: The end of the institutional caliphate
nodes.full: The killing of al-Musta'sim ended the caliphate as a functioning institution. In 1261 the Mamluks installed an Abbasid refugee in Cairo as a titular caliph, kept as a source of legitimacy with no power at all.

nodes.label: The making of the ulama class
nodes.full: The madrasa, the endowed stipend, the licence to transmit and the years of travel in search of teachers turned the scholars into a professional estate — self-reproducing, funded largely by waqf, and increasingly tied to the state.

nodes.label: The women traditionists of Damascus and Baghdad
nodes.full: Women held a recognised place in the transmission of hadith: the long-lived, respected female authority whose short chain of transmitters made her isnad valuable, sought out by male scholars for a licence.

nodes.label: The fida'i and the legend of the Assassins
nodes.full: The Nizari 'devotees' who carried out the killings were the objects of a lurid legend — a secret garden, a drugged paradise. The reality was a besieged minority using targeted killing because it had no army.

nodes.label: The mamluk household
nodes.full: By this period the enslaved-soldier household was the basic unit of Islamic politics: a commander bought and raised boys who became his loyal officers and, on his death, his faction — routes to the highest power for men of servile origin.

nodes.label: The beloved and the jurist — a continuing tension
nodes.full: The love of a beautiful youth remained a central theme of Persian and Arabic poetry — even as the jurists held the act of liwat a capital crime and the Sufis debated whether gazing at a beautiful face was worship or sin.

nodes.label: The human toll of the Mongol conquest
nodes.full: The sources give city death-tolls in the hundreds of thousands or more — figures modern historians cut but do not dismiss. The conquest broke the demographic and agricultural base of the eastern Islamic world for a century.

nodes.label: The conquest stocks the slave markets — and makes the Mamluk state
nodes.full: The Mongol shattering of the Qipchaq Turks threw tens of thousands of steppe people onto the slave markets. Bought and shipped south, they were the manpower al-Salih Ayyub used to raise a new elite regiment — which in 1250 killed the last Ayyubid and founded the Mamluk Sultanate.
